sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Context**: Post-Quit India Movement, Congress leaders were in jail, and the political landscape was stagnant. 
• **The Proposal**: An interim government consisting of equal number of persons nominated by Congress and League in the Central Legislature, with 20% reserved for minorities. 
• **The Commander-in-Chief**: The proposal suggested the Commander-in-Chief would remain an appointee of the British Government. 
• **Key Metric**: The pact was an 'unofficial' effort; neither Gandhi nor Jinnah officially endorsed it initially, leading to its eventual rejection.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Desire to break the 1942-45 political deadlock
Prelims: Distinguish from official Wavell Plan
Equal representation (50:50) for Congress and League
Parity principle to appease Muslim League demands
Mains: Analysis of 'Parity' as a precursor to partition politics

items.definition: The demand for equal representation of Congress and Muslim League in the executive, which became a major bone of contention in subsequent negotiations.
The platform where the pact was negotiated; it served as the primary arena for constitutional maneuvering during the war years.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Breakthrough Attempt**: Aimed to facilitate the release of Congress Working Committee members. 
• **Wavell's Role**: Lord Wavell was aware of the talks and encouraged them to facilitate the Simla Conference.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Jinnah disowned the pact, claiming Liaquat acted without authorization; Congress leadership was wary of the 'parity' clause. 
• **Outcome**: The pact failed to materialize, leading to the more formal but equally unsuccessful Simla Conference.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'D-L-P' (Desai-Liaquat-Pact) = 'Deadlock-Limited-Parity'. 
• **Decoded Meaning**: D (Deadlock breaker attempt), L (Liaquat/League involvement), P (Parity principle).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often frames questions suggesting the Desai-Liaquat Pact was an official agreement signed by the Congress and Muslim League parties. It was NOT; it was an individual initiative by Bhulabhai Desai.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Constitutional Parity' to describe the shift in power-sharing dynamics between 1944-1946.

keyTakeaways: The pact was an unofficial attempt to resolve the political deadlock of 1945.
It introduced the concept of 'parity' between Congress and the Muslim League.
It was ultimately rejected by both Jinnah and the Congress High Command, paving the way for the Simla Conference.
